title: Shimano Sells Not One Bike. So How Does It Make ¥466.2 Billion a Year?
description:
In February 1921, in Sakai, Osaka Prefecture, a young man opened an ironworks, and the next year it began making freewheels for bicycle rear wheels. More than a hundred years later, Nikkei estimates that about 85 percent of the world's sports bike components come from this company, yet it does not sell a single complete bicycle. In 2025 its revenue was 466.2 billion yen: about three quarters from bicycle components and nearly a quarter from fishing tackle.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. The people in them are unidentified ordinary figures; the founder, members of the Shimano family and any logos are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-31

chapters.open-you: The parts maker that sells no bikes
chapters.boom-surge: At 100 years old, revenue up 44 percent
chapters.bust-freeze: 2023: the boom turns to a freeze
chapters.close-question: The business that never competes with its customers

t001.text: Your road bike: when you shift gears mid-ride, that derailleur likely comes from one Japanese company.

t002.text: The company is called Shimano, after its founder's family name.

t003.text: Nikkei estimates it makes about 85 percent of the world's sports bike parts.

t004.text: But here's the surprise: it doesn't sell a single complete bike.

t005.text: Even so, counting fishing tackle, its 2025 revenue still came to 466.2 billion yen.

t006.text: Stranger still, the ride wasn't smooth: in the pandemic years, one bike maker said its parts took 400 days to arrive.

t007.text: And a US product safety commission came knocking.

t008.text: So today, let's talk about it: Shimano sells no bikes, so how do other people's bikes make money for it?

t009.text: Our story starts in February 1921, in Sakai, Osaka Prefecture.

t010.text: Sakai's city government says that about 1,600 years ago, a huge cluster of burial mounds was built here.

t011.text: The metalworking skill behind those mounds later went into guns and kitchen knives.

t012.text: In the Meiji era, what did that craft fix next?

t014.text: From ancient tombs to bicycles. When I first read that, I did a double take.

t015.text: One corporate history says that right here in this city, a 26-year-old opened an ironworks with a single lathe.

t016.text: His name was Shozaburo Shimano. An American dictionary of company histories says he skipped farming with his father to apprentice at an ironworks.

t017.text: In year two, it began making a bike part. Which one?

t019.text: It's why your wheels keep spinning when you stop pedaling.

t020.text: In 1951, it merged with a company called Shimano Bicycle.

t021.text: Bicycle is right there in the name. So why doesn't it sell bikes now?

t022.text: What Shimano Bicycle made isn't on record. What we can find is a different clue.

t023.text: Singapore's Straits Times quoted a Shimano relative:

t024.text: The founder said: never, ever compete with your customers.

t025.text: Nobody can say what year he said it. The founder died in 1958, but those words stayed.

t026.text: If you were a bike maker, would you buy parts from a rival that sells bikes too?

t027.text: I'm guessing no. But that's my guess; the record only has that one line.

t028.text: One corporate history notes that all six presidents to date have been from the Shimano family.

t029.text: But if you only make parts and never compete, where are the customers?

t030.text: Overseas. In March 1965, it opened a company in New York.

t031.text: In 1967, a German company became its sole distributor in Germany.

t032.text: Remember that German company. It shows up again at the very end of the story.

t033.text: In 1970, it also started making something with nothing to do with bikes: fishing reels.

t034.text: You heard that right, fishing. How big that side business grows, we'll get to later.

t036.text: In 1972, Americans bought more bicycles than cars.

t037.text: In 1973, it opened its first assembly plant outside Japan, in Singapore.

t038.text: One veteran American mechanic wrote that its top-tier groupset, Dura-Ace, already had that name in 1973.

t039.text: But the groupset didn't truly take off until 1984.

t041.text: In 1984, it put something new on Dura-Ace: indexed shifting.

t042.text: Before, shifting was done by feel. Indexed means one click, one gear.

t043.text: Today, when one click puts you right in gear, that's this idea.

t044.text: But others made good parts too. So what was its edge?

t045.text: Its edge was how it sold. The same dictionary says it matched shifters and derailleurs into one full set,

t046.text: and sold the whole set to bike makers. In my view, that move beat any single new part.

t047.text: It didn't sell the bike. But that whole set of parts on it? It sold that.

t048.text: With the whole set covered, how could anyone else's parts get in?

t049.text: In 1987, a new company called SRAM popped up in Chicago, making twist shifters.

t050.text: That small company sued Shimano in California under antitrust law.

t051.text: In 1991, the two settled out of court, on undisclosed terms.

t052.text: After that, bike makers could mix other brands' parts.

t053.text: In the early 1990s, it also put shifting and braking in one lever.

t054.text: In 1997, the US Consumer Product Safety Commission issued a notice. The star: a crank.

t055.text: The crank is the metal arm that turns along with you when you pedal.

t056.text: The notice said over a million of these cranks were on bikes in North America,

t057.text: with more than 630 reports of breaks and 22 people injured.

t058.text: Whose bikes were these cranks on?

t059.text: Over 200 models, under at least 49 brands.

t060.text: One name on the list you'll definitely know: Giant.

t061.text: To me, this is the flip side of everyone using it: when one part fails, every brand fails together.

t062.text: But it wasn't over. Remember that commission from the start? In 1999, it came knocking.

t063.text: Shimano's US arm agreed to pay a $150,000 civil penalty.

t064.text: Stranger still, the charge wasn't that cranks broke. It was reporting late:

t065.text: it knew people were hurt but didn't report in time.

t066.text: Shimano denied any crank defect and any breach of its reporting duty.

t067.text: I'd guess that sum barely stung. But keep that number; we'll compare it to another fine.

t068.text: What really put it on a roller coaster was 2020.

t069.text: When the pandemic hit, demand for bikes suddenly shot up. That August, a Nikkei column ran this headline:

t070.text: This bike parts maker was now worth more than Nissan Motor.

t071.text: A gear maker worth more than a carmaker. I read that headline twice.

t073.text: Remember those 400 days from the start? This was it.

t074.text: The FT quoted Western bike makers: high-end parts took that long from order to shipment.

t075.text: If you tried to buy a new bike back then and got told to wait, this was part of why.

t077.text: Its PR said capacity had been greatly expanded,

t078.text: output in the fourth quarter of 2020 was the highest in company history, and customers should order as early as possible.

t079.text: In 2021 it turned 100. Revenue rose 44 percent, and operating profit nearly 80 percent.

t080.text: The new president told Nikkei it would invest about 20 billion yen in a new plant in Singapore.

t081.text: How high did the boom go?

t082.text: In 2022, revenue soared to 628.9 billion yen.

t083.text: Back in 2019, before the pandemic, it was 363.2 billion.

t084.text: With business like that, you'd think the good times would never end.

t085.text: That October, its earnings report added one line: demand was fairly steady, but showing signs of cooling.

t086.text: Cooling soon turned into a freeze. In 2023, revenue fell by almost a quarter,

t087.text: operating profit was cut in half, and bike parts dropped nearly 30 percent.

t088.text: The report said: the boom had cooled, but market stock was still too high; North American retail sales of complete bikes stayed weak.

t089.text: Picture it: parts ordered in a pandemic frenzy, built into bikes, sitting in warehouses and shops, with no buyers.

t090.text: Remember that new Singapore plant? Of all years, it started running in this one.

t091.text: A decision made in the boom arrived in the freeze.

t092.text: On September 21 that same year, the commission issued another recall notice. A crank again.

t093.text: This time it was 11-speed bonded hollow cranks, and the problem was separation.

t095.text: 680,000 sets in the US, plus 80,000 in Canada.

t096.text: The notice listed 4,519 reports of cranks separating.

t097.text: These cranks sold for over 11 years, at $270 to $1,500 a set.

t098.text: If you bought one of its pricier cranks in those years, this notice is worth looking up.

t100.text: Free inspections alone meant a 17.6 billion yen loss that year.

t101.text: So here's the question: did it really not see this crash coming?

t102.text: It did. In 2024, chairman Yozo Shimano told Nikkei: we knew all along it would crash someday.

t104.text: He said at the peak, all they could do was push output and delay other plans.

t105.text: In 2024, revenue slipped a bit more. At this point, you might think it's headed down for good.

t106.text: But in 2025, revenue rose 3.4 percent, to that 466.2 billion from the start.

t107.text: Remember those fishing reels from 1970? This year, fishing made up nearly a quarter of revenue.

t108.text: But operating profit fell 20 percent, so it earned less than revenue suggests.

t109.text: Who bought the most from it?

t110.text: In its annual report, the biggest-customer line shows a German name.

t111.text: Remember the company that became its German distributor in 1967?

t112.text: It's called Paul Lange, based in Stuttgart, founded in 1949.

t113.text: In 2025, that one company bought almost 54 billion yen from Shimano,

t114.text: 11.6 percent of revenue, making it Shimano's biggest customer.

t115.text: I didn't see this answer coming either: a year earlier it was under 10 percent, not even named in the report.

t116.text: In one year, revenue from Germany rose almost 40 percent, while China fell by a third.

t117.text: But the story isn't over yet. In 2026, two threads from earlier came back together.

t118.text: Remember order as early as possible? On March 1, Nikkei put it more bluntly:

t119.text: Shimano couldn't talk bike makers out of overbuilding in the boom.

t120.text: In my view, this is the hardest part of making parts: customers build the bikes, and how many isn't your call.

t121.text: Then came that commission from the start. On March 16, it was back.

t122.text: Shimano agreed to pay an $11.5 million civil penalty.

t124.text: Exactly the same as in 1999: not reporting right away.

t125.text: Twenty-seven years apart. That's what bugs me most in this whole file.

t126.text: This time, Shimano's settlement states that it doesn't admit the allegations.

t127.text: It also says no consumer injuries were reported once inspections began.

t128.text: That $150,000 from before became more than 70 times bigger.

t129.text: Back to our question: it sells no bikes, so how does it do it?

t130.text: My answer: remember the founder's words, never compete with your customers?

t131.text: Because it doesn't compete, bike makers trust it and put its parts on their bikes,

t132.text: and distributors sell its parts into markets like Germany.

t133.text: But there's another side. Remember that 1997 crank? Everyone used it, so everyone got hit;

t134.text: and in a boom, can it stop bike makers from overbuilding?

t136.text: Selling no bikes lets it profit from everyone's bikes, and rise and fall along with them.

t137.text: Well, that's today's story. Whose derailleur is on your bike? Tell me in the comments.

t138.text: Every file comes with sources. To keep digging with us, subscribe.
